scenario: A customer-support lead wants every agent's Claude chats to follow the same returns policy and reply style.
question: What is the best setup?
options: Ask each agent to paste the policy at the start of every chat
A shared Project with the returns policy as knowledge and the reply rules as Project instructions
Put the returns policy in each agent's account instructions
Use an incognito chat so the policy isn't stored
explanation: B is correct: a Project bundles instructions and knowledge so every chat in it starts from the same rules and documents, and it can be shared with the team. A is wrong because repeated pasting is error-prone and inconsistent. C is wrong because account instructions apply to all of a person's chats and aren't meant for reference documents. D is wrong because incognito chats aren't available in Projects and keep nothing.

scenario: A team on a paid plan keeps adding documents to a Project, and its knowledge is approaching the context limit.
question: What happens?
options: The Project deletes the oldest files
The Project stops accepting chats
Retrieval (RAG) switches on automatically, letting the Project hold much more knowledge by searching it for the relevant parts
Claude reads only the first file
explanation: C is correct: on paid plans, Projects switch to retrieval automatically as knowledge nears the context limit, expanding capacity (up to about ten times). A is wrong because files aren't deleted. B is wrong because chats continue normally. D is wrong because retrieval searches across the knowledge.

scenario: On a Team plan, a manager wants colleagues to use her Project but not change its instructions or files.
question: Which sharing option fits?
options: Share the Project with "Can view" access
Share it with "Can edit" access
Copy the instructions into each colleague's account settings
Make the Project public on the internet
explanation: A is correct: "Can view" lets colleagues use the Project without changing its setup. B is wrong because edit access lets them change instructions and knowledge. C is wrong because copies drift and aren't maintained in one place. D is wrong because company Projects shouldn't be exposed publicly.

scenario: An executive assistant exports the boss's calendar to a file and uploads it to a Project every morning.
question: What is the better approach?
options: Connect Google Calendar so Claude can read the live schedule from the connected account
Upload the calendar twice a day instead
Paste the calendar into the Project instructions
Ask Claude to guess the schedule from previous weeks
explanation: A is correct: connectors suit information that changes often, such as calendars and email. B is wrong because more uploads are still stale snapshots. C is wrong because instructions are for rules, not daily data. D is wrong because guessing a schedule produces wrong answers.

scenario: With Gmail connected, Claude drafts a reply to a client.
question: What happens by default before the email is sent?
options: Claude sends it immediately without asking
Claude sends it from a shared company account
Claude asks for the user's approval before sending
Claude forwards it to the user's manager for approval
explanation: C is correct: by default, connector actions such as sending email ask for approval first. A is wrong because sending isn't automatic by default. B is wrong because a connector acts only for the connected account. D is wrong because Claude doesn't route approvals to managers.

scenario: A team member connects Google Drive and asks Claude to summarise a document that only her manager can access.
question: What should she expect?
options: Claude can read any document in the company's Drive
Claude can access only what her connected account can access, so it can't read the manager's private document
Claude will request the file from the manager automatically
Claude will summarise it from the document's title
explanation: B is correct: connectors only reach the connected account's data and permissions. A is wrong because connectors don't bypass sharing permissions. C is wrong because Claude doesn't request access on her behalf. D is wrong because summarising from a title would be guessing.

scenario: A consultant wants every Claude chat to use British spelling and lead with the recommendation, whatever the topic.
question: Where should this preference go?
options: The instructions of one client Project
A knowledge file in every Project
The first message of each chat
Account instructions, which apply to all of her chats
explanation: D is correct: preferences that apply everywhere belong in account instructions. A is wrong because Project instructions apply only within that Project. B is wrong because knowledge files are reference material, not rules. C is wrong because repeating it in every chat is what standing instructions avoid.

scenario: A bid team is writing the instructions for its client-proposals Project.
question: Which Project instruction is most effective?
options: "Be professional and good."
"Write for procurement managers. Lead with cost and timeline. Use the attached template's headings. If a requirement is unclear, list it under 'Questions for the client' rather than assuming."
"Never make any mistakes."
"Write proposals."
explanation: B is correct: effective instructions are specific and positive, name the audience and structure, and say what to do when information is missing. A is wrong because it's too vague to change behaviour. C is wrong because it isn't something Claude can act on. D is wrong because it adds nothing about how.

scenario: A user's account instructions say "always answer in bullet points", but a Project requires full paragraphs for client letters. Results are inconsistent.
question: What is the best fix?
options: Add the same rule to the Project three times so it wins
Delete the Project
Ask Claude to choose whichever format it prefers
Make the instructions consistent: make the account preference conditional or remove it, and keep the letter format in the Project instructions
explanation: D is correct: conflicting standing instructions at different levels cause inconsistent output; each rule should sit at the level where it applies. A is wrong because repetition doesn't resolve a conflict. B is wrong because the Project is useful. C is wrong because it leaves the format unpredictable.

scenario: A pricing policy changes. The Project now holds both the old and the new pricing file.
question: What should the Project owner do?
options: Remove the old file, keep the single current version, and note the change in the instructions
Keep both so nothing is lost
Rename the new file "FINAL" and keep both
Tell users to ignore the old file
explanation: A is correct: one current version avoids Claude using conflicting sources. B is wrong because Claude may draw from either version. C is wrong because a file name doesn't stop Claude reading the old file. D is wrong because users can't control which file Claude uses.

scenario: A shared Project is used by 40 people. Nobody has checked its files since it was created a year ago.
question: Which practice best keeps it reliable?
options: Let anyone add files whenever they like
Delete the Project every year and start again
Assign an owner, set a review schedule, and test with a few standard questions after each update
Wait for users to complain
explanation: C is correct: an owner, a review schedule and testing keep a shared configuration current. A is wrong because unmanaged edits create duplicates and conflicts. B is wrong because it throws away good setup. D is wrong because a stale Project fails quietly, answering confidently from old information.

scenario: The owner of a team Project updates the leave policy file and the instructions.
question: What else should she do?
options: Nothing; users will notice the answers changed
Ask users to re-upload the old policy in their chats
Test the Project with common leave questions and tell users what changed
Turn off memory for the whole team
explanation: C is correct: after changes, test that answers are right and inform users so they know what changed. A is wrong because silent changes confuse users. B is wrong because it brings back outdated information. D is wrong because memory isn't related to the policy update.
